query: What exact approach will we use to handle dependent effect sizes: preferred multilevel variance structure, RVE settings, Bayesian priors for variance components, and sensitivity thresholds for dependence handling?

response.query: What exact approach will we use to handle dependent effect sizes: preferred multilevel variance structure, RVE settings, Bayesian priors for variance components, and sensitivity thresholds for dependence handling?
response.answer: To handle dependent effect sizes, use multilevel models with robust variance estimation and specify a sampling error variance-covariance matrix. Bayesian priors and sensitivity thresholds can also be applied for variance components and dependence handling.

results.content: Meta-analysis is the use of statistical methods to combine the results of individual studies to estimate the overall effect size for a specific outcome of interest. RVE makes no assumption about the specific form of effect sizes' sampling distributions and requires no information about the covariate structure of dependent effect sizes, making it advantageous over other methods such as generalized least squares estimation and multilevel meta-analysis (Hedges et al., 2010;Tanner-Smith & Tipton, 2014). This method allows researchers to estimate meta-regression models with dependent effect sizes; however, when used with small samples, it can produce narrow confidence intervals and, thus, increase the chances of a type I error (Hedges et al., 2010;Tanner-Smith & Tipton, 2014;Tipton, 2013). Meta-analysis: mean effect size.-To obtain the mean effect size for each category in each model, we used a robust variance meta-regression (Tipton 2013), with a random effect of study area to account for heterogeneity among effect sizes from different sites (Borenstein et al. Given one of our objectives was to determine whether generalized fish-flow relationships could be identified from the available literature [which would include null hypothesis testing regarding heterogeneity parameters (e.g., Q test to determine whether individual effect sizes estimate a common population mean)], and our small database of studies for quantitative analysis in CI and BA replication type subsets, we were limited in our ability to use other approaches such as robust variance estimation or multi-level meta-analysis [45][46][47][48][49]. This approach accounts for the within-cluster correlation of effect sizes via robust estimation of sample weights and standard errors, thus removing the requirement for only one effect to be used per study per meta-analysis and maximising the available data for analysis (Hedges et al., 2010;Tanner-Smith et al., 2016;Tanner-Smith and Tipton, 2014;Tipton, 2013). Robust variance estimation has advantages over other statistical methods that can also handle within-study dependence, such as generalized least squares estimation (Gleser and Olkin, 2009) and multilevel meta-analysis model (Van den Noortgate et al., 2013), because it makes no assumption about the specific form of effect sizes' sampling distributions and requires no information about the covariate structure of dependent effect sizes Tanner-Smith and Tipton, 2014).

results.title: Modelling approaches for meta‐analyses with dependent effect sizes in ecology and evolution: A simulation study - Williams - 2025 - Methods in Ecology and Evolution - Wiley Online Library
results.content: We assessed the performance of multilevel models, incorporating an assumed sampling error variance–covariance (VCV) matrix (which account for within-study correlation), cluster robust variance estimation (CRVE) methods and their combination across different true within-study correlations. In a recent study, Pustejovsky and Tipton (2022) proposed a new working model that combines multilevel meta-analytical models, an assumed sampling error VCV matrix, and CRVE, with simulations demonstrating that this approach enhances the precision of regression estimates. In this paper, we conduct a simulation study to evaluate the performance of different meta-analysis modelling approaches to account for dependence in effect sizes and sampling errors. We compare two approaches under different working models: one that specifies a within-study error VCV matrix assuming constant correlation, and another that incorporates a cluster robust variance estimator (CRVE) in the context of ecological and evolutionary data. We considered three values of true constant within-study correlation among effect sizes, fixed across studies, to reflect different levels of dependence and to match models with assumed sampling error matrix structures. #### 3.2.2 Phylogenetic multilevel meta-regression For the phylogenetic meta-regression model, the estimates of the four coefficients (, study level , species level and effect size level ) were unbiased and did not vary across models with different within-study correlations (Figures S12–S15; Table S9). Regarding multilevel phylogenetic meta-analyses (Study 2), our simulation results found the overall mean estimates were unbiased across all models with and without a specified sampling () matrix, also shown in Van den Noortgate et al. ### 4.2 Variance component estimates When we assumed a sampling error matrix that matched the true underlying data-generating mechanisms the multilevel meta-analysis models in both simulation studies provided unbiased estimates of the within and among study variance components. Specifically, we advocate the use of multilevel models to explicitly account for heterogeneity at every relevant hierarchical level, use advised inference methods, and incorporate a sampling error variance–covariance matrix using any known values of correlations among effect sizes from primary studies to obtain accurate variance component estimates. A simulation study of cluster robust variance estimation methods and modelling approaches for meta-analyses with dependent effect sizes in ecology and evolution.

results.content: The second step achieves estimates of standard errors consistent with the multilevel meta-analytic model, a benchmark method with adequate control of Type I error rates for multiple, statistically dependent effect sizes. In many disciplines, the multilevel meta-analysis (MLMA) model has become a standard (benchmark) method for dealing with dependent effect sizes due to its flexible random-effects structure (Yang et al., 2022). In the first step, we incorporate a bias-robust weighting scheme into a meta-analytic model (i.e. bias-robust model) to obtain less biased estimates of mean effect sizes in the presence of selective reporting. However, while the FE + VCV model can reduce the bias of with respect to selective reporting, is underestimated due to the failure to account for multiple, statistically dependent effect sizes (effect sizes are arbitrarily correlated within the same study), distorting statistical inference and inflating test statistic , and Type I error rate (thus reducing *p*-value). #### 2.3.3 Detecting selective reporting using multilevel Egger's test and ad hoc selection model Detecting selective reporting in the presence of dependent effect sizes poses a challenge, particularly in our dataset of 448 meta-analyses, as most methods violate the assumption of statistical independence (Nakagawa et al., 2022). ### 3.2 Inflation of the mean effect size if ignoring selective reporting In the presence of selective reporting, as identified by MLMA Egger, the overall effects estimated by the benchmark method (MLMA model), consistently exceeded those obtained from the first step bias-robust model of our proposed method (FE + VCV; Figure 3).
